question: What is the main purpose of a decision log during a crisis?
options: To record who decided what, on what information and assumptions, so decisions can be revisited, handed over and later explained honestly
To slow decisions down
To replace the incident timeline
To meet a SOC 2 requirement
explain: A decision log makes uncertainty explicit and decisions reviewable. It is also the best defence against later claims that something was hidden, because it shows what was known at the time.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Plain, direct and first: sentences a busy reader acts on
question: Which sentence follows the plain language guidance best for a message to a service owner?
options: Your login service accepts expired session tokens; please deploy the fix in pull request 812 by Wednesday.
It is recommended that remediation of the identified issue be performed in a timely manner.
Remediation should be considered by the relevant stakeholders.
A potential weakness may exist in some authentication components.
explain: It is active, present tense, names the system, the defect, the action and the deadline. The others are passive, use hidden verbs ('remediation be performed') and leave out who and when.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Executive summaries: one page for the person who decides
question: Which sentence belongs in an executive summary?
options: An attacker on the internet can take control of the main firewall; the vendor fix takes about an hour to apply and should be applied today.
We used Nmap 7.95 and Burp Suite to enumerate the attack surface.
CVE-2024-3400 was observed on the edge firewall.
The team worked hard over two weeks.
explain: It states the consequence in business terms, the cost of fixing it and the urgency. Tool names, bare CVE numbers and effort statements belong elsewhere or nowhere.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Design-review and code-review comments that get acted on
question: Which review comment is most likely to get a correct fix quickly?
options: issue (security, blocking): /export joins a user-supplied path to the reports directory, so ../ can reach other files. Could we resolve it and check it stays inside? Helper: docs/safe-paths.md
Insecure. Fix.
Why would anyone build it like this?
nitpick: path handling
explain: It is labelled and blocking, locates the defect, gives the scenario, proposes a specific fix and points to a helper. The others give no reason, attack the author, or understate a real issue as a nitpick.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
question: Why does training the policy head on MCTS visit counts improve the network instead of just copying it?
options: Visit counts are smoother than the prior, so the cross-entropy loss is lower
The search samples at a higher temperature, so the targets are more diverse
The search mixes the prior with measured look-ahead values, so the visit counts differ from the prior where look-ahead finds better moves
The visit counts include moves from human expert games
explain: The search is an improvement operator: it starts from the prior and moves visits toward moves whose measured values are higher. In the toy, the prior said 0.30 for b and the search said 0.889. Imitating that difference is the improvement. AlphaZero uses no human games.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: When the filter lies: lucky answers, proxy rewards, overfitting
question: For which task would a STaR-style final-answer filter keep the fewest flawed rationales, for the same model accuracy?
options: True or false questions
5-way multiple choice questions
Competition math problems with an integer answer
Open-ended summaries scored by a learned reward model
explain: The flawed share depends on c, the chance a flawed attempt matches anyway. It is 0.5 for true or false, 0.2 for 5 options, and tiny for an integer answer. A learned reward model adds its own errors on top, as ReST's human evaluation showed.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Adversarial self-play for language models, and AlphaProof
question: In R-Zero, the Solver answers a new question 10 times. Which outcome puts the question in the Solver's training set?
options: 10 of 10 answers agree, so the label is surely right
1 of 10 agree, the hardest kind of question
5 of 10 agree, inside the 3 to 7 band
Any outcome, as long as a Python executor validates the question
explain: R-Zero keeps a question only if 3 to 7 of the 10 answers match the majority-vote pseudo-label: not trivially easy, and not so uncertain that the majority answer is likely to be wrong. There is no executor; the label is the model's own vote.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Provider prompt caching is a different thing from semantic caching
question: Which of the two can return an answer that is wrong for the current question even though the model would have answered correctly?
options: Provider prompt caching
Neither, since both check the full prompt
Semantic caching
Both equally
explain: Prompt caching only skips recomputing an identical prefix; the answer is still generated for the full current prompt. A semantic cache returns an answer generated for a different prompt, and a false hit is exactly that failure.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Why cloud metadata is the prize: Capital One 2019
question: Capital One's WAF role could list and read every bucket. Which single change would have limited the damage most, even if the SSRF still worked?
options: Moving the WAF to a different AWS region
Rotating the role's credentials every hour instead of every few hours
Giving the WAF role only the permissions a firewall needs, with no S3 read access
Encrypting the HTTP traffic between the WAF and IMDS
explain: Least privilege bounds what stolen credentials can do. Faster rotation still leaves minutes to hours of valid keys, the region changes nothing, and IMDS traffic never leaves the instance, so encrypting it would not stop a relayed request.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: XML, entities and XXE
question: Which change most completely removes XXE and billion-laughs risk in a Java service that never uses DTDs?
options: Block requests containing the word ENTITY
Return generic error messages
Set disallow-doctype-decl to true on the parser factory
Validate the XML against a schema after parsing
explain: Without a DOCTYPE no entities can be declared, so neither external fetches nor expansion bombs are possible. Generic errors only hide the output (blind XXE still works), keyword filters are fragile, and schema validation happens after the parser has already expanded entities.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Path traversal and safe path joins
question: `safe = os.path.join(BASE, name); if not safe.startswith(BASE): reject`. Which input still escapes?
options: report.txt
subdir/report.txt
An empty string
../files-backup/secret.txt when BASE is /srv/app/files
explain: join does not normalise, but even after normalising, /srv/app/files-backup/secret.txt starts with the string /srv/app/files. String prefixes are not path prefixes. Compare whole components (commonpath in Python, Path.startsWith in Java, or BASE plus a separator in Node).

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: LM programs: why the runtime should see the whole program
question: In `tip_suggestion`, what happens when Python executes `f += sgl.gen(...)` for fork 0?
options: Python blocks until fork 0's paragraph is fully generated, then moves to fork 1
Both forks are concatenated into a single request with one long prompt
The call is submitted to fork 0's stream and returns at once, so fork 1 is submitted right away and the runtime can batch them
The function is compiled into a CUDA graph before any request is sent
explain: The interpreter runs each prompt state as an asynchronous stream: `gen` is non-blocking, like a kernel launch. Only reading a result (`forks[0]["detailed_tip"]`) waits. That is what gives intra-program parallelism.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Structured output today: grammar masks inside the SGLang scheduler
question: A service sends 10,000 requests, each with a different, freshly generated JSON schema, and sees much higher time to first token than with one fixed schema. What is the most likely cause?
options: The radix cache cannot store JSON outputs
Masks for unique schemas are computed on the GPU instead of the CPU
XGrammar falls back to jump-forward decoding for new schemas
Every request waits in the grammar queue for its own compilation, because the grammar cache only helps when a schema repeats
explain: Compilation is per distinct constraint and runs before the request can be scheduled. A fixed schema compiles once and then hits the cache. Reusing schemas (for example, generating them from a few templates) removes the cost.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Turning a road map into a weighted directed graph
question: In the toy graph, a planner picks the route with the fewest roads and breaks ties arbitrarily. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing; fewest roads always means fastest when weights are minutes
It may return S, C, F, T (14 min) even though S, D, F, T takes 9 min
It cannot find any route, because BFS ignores weights entirely
It always returns the slowest 3-road route
explain: Three routes tie at 3 roads (9, 10 and 14 minutes). Hop count ignores weights, so any of them can come out. We need an algorithm that compares accumulated minutes, which is exactly what Dijkstra's algorithm does.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
question: A travel time function says: leave at 08:05 and arrive at 08:30.6, or leave at 08:10 and arrive at 08:27.4. What does this violate, and why does it matter?
options: Admissibility; A* would overestimate
Nonnegative weights; travel times went negative
FIFO; waiting would beat leaving now, which breaks the label-setting search for earliest arrival
Turn restrictions; the profile is missing a penalty
explain: Leaving later and arriving earlier violates FIFO. Then arriving at a node as early as possible no longer guarantees arriving as early as possible further along, so a settled earliest-arrival label can be wrong. Dijkstra-style time-dependent search assumes FIFO, and the survey notes that other settings are studied separately.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: IIR filters, zero-phase filtering and real sensor data
question: A drone's control loop needs a filtered gyro reading every 1 ms. Someone proposes `sosfiltfilt` because it has zero phase delay. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; zero phase is ideal for control
sosfiltfilt only works on FIR filters
sosfiltfilt runs the filter backward from the end of the signal, so it needs future samples and cannot run in real time
sosfiltfilt halves the filter order, so it filters too weakly
explain: The backward pass starts from the last sample, which a real-time loop does not have yet. Real-time systems must use a causal filter (sosfilt, or an FIR) and accept or compensate its delay. Forward-backward filtering doubles the effective order; it does not halve it.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Masks instead of branches: compares, blends and AVX-512
question: In AVX-512, `r = _mm512_mask_add_ps(src, k, a, b)` with k = 0x0003. What are lanes 0 and 5 of r?
options: Lane 0 = a0 + b0, lane 5 = 0
Lane 0 = src0, lane 5 = a5 + b5
Both lanes are a + b; k only affects stores
Lane 0 = a0 + b0, lane 5 = src5
explain: 0x0003 sets bits 0 and 1, so lanes 0 and 1 get a + b. The mask_ form is merge masking: inactive lanes copy src. The maskz_ form would have produced 0 in lane 5.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Why a general-purpose heap wastes memory
question: Why does a program not simply call `mmap` for every 24-byte object?
options: mmap cannot return memory smaller than a page, and each call is a system call, so it is both wasteful and slow
mmap memory cannot be written to until it is passed through malloc
mmap always returns memory on a different NUMA node
mmap regions are freed automatically after one function returns
explain: mmap works in whole pages (4 KiB on typical x86-64) and costs a kernel entry per call. An allocator amortizes both costs by carving many small objects out of one mapping. (A NUMA node, a group of CPUs with its own local memory on a non-uniform memory access machine, has nothing to do with it.)

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Three modules, one loop: how slime is laid out
question: You want to raise SGLang's KV cache budget inside a slime run. SGLang's own flag is `--mem-fraction-static`. What do you pass to slime's train.py?
options: `--sglang-mem-fraction-static 0.8`
`--mem-fraction-static 0.8`, since slime forwards unknown flags
Nothing: slime fixes SGLang memory internally
`--rollout-mem-fraction 0.8`
explain: SGLang arguments are passed through with a `--sglang-` prefix. Unprefixed flags are interpreted as Megatron or slime arguments, and there is no slime-specific rollout memory flag.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Generating data: the rollout loop and your own functions
question: Your agent calls a code interpreter between model turns and appends the interpreter output to the response. Training loss starts rewarding the model for "predicting" interpreter output. What is the bug?
options: The reward function should return a list
You need --rollout-function-path instead of a custom generate function
The router should be bypassed for tool calls
Tool output tokens were appended with trainable=True instead of trainable=False, so they are in the loss mask
explain: Only model-generated tokens should carry loss. The search-r1 example appends observation tokens with `trainable=False` (loss mask 0). Swapping hook types does not fix a wrong mask.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Is the run working? Evaluation, metrics, checkpoints and recovery
question: A fully async agentic run sets `--eval-interval 20` and an AIME eval set, but no eval/ metrics ever appear. Why, and what should you do?
options: Eval runs only every 20 epochs
The eval set must be Parquet
--n-samples-per-eval-prompt defaults to 0
The fully async rollout implements no evaluation, so evaluate saved checkpoints in a separate job
explain: The experiment guide and the fully async README both say the continuous queue does not implement evaluation, which would conflict with the continuously running model. Evaluate saved checkpoints separately. --n-samples-per-eval-prompt defaults to 1.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Inside the EVM: storage, calls, msg.sender and delegatecall
question: Ana calls contract A, which calls contract B. Inside B, what are msg.sender and tx.origin?
options: msg.sender = Ana, tx.origin = A
Both are Ana
Both are A
msg.sender = A, tx.origin = Ana
explain: msg.sender is the immediate caller (A); tx.origin is the EOA that signed the transaction (Ana). Authorising on tx.origin lets any contract Ana calls act as Ana.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Unchecked external calls and denial of service
question: Which line has an unchecked external call?
options: to.call{value: amt}("");
require(token.transfer(to, amt));
(bool ok, ) = to.call{value: amt}(""); require(ok);
payable(to).transfer(amt);
explain: A bare low-level call returns false on failure and execution continues. The other lines either check the result or (transfer) revert automatically.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Bridges: where many of the largest DeFi thefts happened
question: A bridge needs 5 of 9 validator signatures. The company runs 4 validators on shared infrastructure, and one partner validator has delegated signing to the company. What is the real number of compromises needed to forge a withdrawal?
options: 5 separate compromises
1: compromising the company's infrastructure reaches all 5 signatures
0, signatures cannot be forged
explain: This was Ronin's situation: one breach of Sky Mavis reached its four validators and, through the stale allowlist, the Axie DAO validator. Threshold security counts independent parties, not keys.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Incident response on chain, and where to practise
question: A team's lending contract has no pause function and no upgrade path. A bug is found that lets anyone drain 1% of funds per transaction. What can the team still do quickly?
options: Patch the contract in place
Little on chain: warn users to withdraw, ask exchanges and issuers to freeze, and coordinate with researchers; the missing pause is the real failure
Roll back the chain
Nothing at all is possible
explain: Without a pause or upgrade path the code keeps running. Response falls back to off-chain actions, which is why pause roles, caps and monitoring belong in the design.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Verdicts, severity and priority: true, false and benign positives
question: Two alerts arrive at once. Alert X: severity critical, on a test VM that holds no data, from a rule that is right 2 percent of the time. Alert Y: severity medium, on the payroll database server, from a rule that is right 40 percent of the time. Which should normally be worked first, and why?
options: Y, because priority weighs severity against asset criticality and the rule's track record, and Y wins on both
X, because critical always beats medium
Whichever arrived first
Neither until both rules are tuned
explain: Severity is only one input. Y sits on a crown-jewel asset and comes from a rule that is right far more often. That is the point of separating severity (bad if true) from priority (what to do now).

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Phishing reports and unusual data egress
question: A laptop's daily upload is normally about 50 MB. Today it sent 4 GB to a well-known cloud storage provider, and the company uses that provider. Which next step best separates exfiltration from normal work?
options: Close it: the provider is sanctioned
Block the provider for the whole company
Find which process and which account did the upload, and whether the destination account belongs to the company's tenant or someone else's
Geolocate the provider's IP address
explain: A sanctioned provider gives cover (T1567.002). The distinguishing facts are the process (the sync client or something odd?) and the destination tenant or account. Geolocation of a cloud provider's IP tells you where their data centre is, nothing more.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: When to escalate, and case notes someone else can act on
question: Why should a case note list what was checked and found clean?
options: To make the note longer
Because auditors only read negative results
It should not; only findings belong in a note
Because negative results bound the scope and stop others from repeating the same checks, or tell them precisely which checks to extend
explain: "No other host contacted the IP in 7 days of proxy logs" is a scope boundary. Without it, IR either repeats the search or wrongly assumes it was done more broadly.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Security is a secondary task: why people work around it
question: Herley argues that ignoring a piece of security advice can be rational. Which condition makes that most likely?
options: The advice costs every user effort every day, while the harm it prevents falls on a small fraction of users
The advice comes from a government agency
The advice protects against a very common attack
The advice is free to follow
explain: A daily cost multiplied across everyone easily exceeds a rare loss to a few. Advice that is cheap, or that prevents frequent and costly harm, does not fit Herley's argument.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a pretext: how manipulation is built and broken
question: In CISA's description of Scattered Spider, what was the purpose of the group's first calls to a help desk?
options: To learn what steps are needed for a password reset, so later calls could follow them convincingly
To install ransomware directly
To test whether phones were monitored
To ask for a job
explain: AA23-320A says the early attempts were designed to learn the reset steps, then later calls gathered details about a target employee. Research calls are a detection opportunity if staff report them.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: SIM swaps, bribed insiders and people you do not employ
question: Which change removes most of the value of a SIM swap against your employees' work accounts?
options: Asking carriers to train their staff
Requiring phishing-resistant MFA and recovery that never relies on SMS or voice
Telling employees to keep their phones charged
Using longer passwords
explain: If codes and resets never go to the phone number, moving the number gains the attacker nothing at work. Carrier rules help, but you cannot control every carrier's staff.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Dropped USB drives, implants and unattended screens
question: The USB study found most people plugged in drives to find the owner. Which awareness message follows from that finding?
options: Give found devices to IT or security; they will return them safely
Never pick up anything you find
Only plug found drives into personal computers
Open only the files that look like documents
explain: The motivation was helpfulness, so the message should redirect it to a safe channel. Plugging into a personal machine still risks the person and anything that machine touches.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Why single neurons are hard to read: superposition
question: A colleague says: 'If a model had 768 dimensions, it could track at most 768 features without errors, so superposition can't help.' What is the best reply?
options: Exact orthogonality caps it at 768, but many sparse features can share almost-orthogonal directions because they rarely fire together, and a ReLU filters small interference.
Right: superposition only works when features are dense and frequently co-occur.
Wrong: 768 dimensions can hold 768 squared exactly orthogonal directions.
Right: that is why language models need one neuron per feature.
explain: Only d directions can be exactly orthogonal, but random directions in 768 dimensions overlap by only about 0.036. When features are sparse, two overlapping features are rarely on together, and a negative bias plus ReLU removes the small leaks. Dense features make collisions common, which is when superposition stops paying.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
question: A residual-stream SAE and an MLP-output SAE in the same layer have the same FVU. Which do you expect to raise the language model's loss more when spliced in, and why?
options: The MLP SAE, because MLP outputs are sparser
Neither: equal FVU means equal downstream loss
The residual-stream SAE, because its error is carried into every later layer, while an MLP error is small next to the whole residual stream
The residual-stream SAE, because residual SAEs have more dead latents
explain: Gemma Scope reports consistently higher delta loss for residual-stream SAEs at similar FVU. FVU measures error relative to that site's own variance; what matters downstream is how big the error is relative to everything later layers read.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: train a TopK SAE on GPT-2, then use a released one
question: You forget to drop position 0 when caching GPT-2 small activations at this site. What is the most likely symptom?
options: Many latents end up dedicated to the few huge BOS vectors, and FVU is dominated by them, while ordinary tokens reconstruct poorly
Nothing: the SAE averages over tokens, so one position cannot matter
The SAE gets more dead latents because BOS vectors are small
Training becomes faster because the BOS vectors are easy
explain: Position 0's norm here is about 38 times the others, so its squared error is over 1,000 times larger. Unnormalised, those vectors dominate the loss and the scale estimate. That is why caches skip BOS, EOS and padding.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in map coordinates
question: Two estimates at the same point: simple kriging with an assumed mean of 13.0 gives 15.090; ordinary kriging gives 15.099. Why do they differ slightly?
options: Ordinary kriging uses a different variogram
Simple kriging ignores the nearest sensor
Simple kriging's weights need not sum to 1, so the assumed mean gets weight 1 minus their sum; ordinary kriging estimates the mean from the data instead
They are numerically unstable; the difference is rounding error
explain: Simple kriging writes the estimate as $m + \sum \lambda_i (z_i - m)$, so the known mean carries the leftover weight (here $1 - 1.042$). Ordinary kriging forces the weights to sum to 1, which is equivalent to using a data-estimated mean (12.80 here).

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution
question: A teammate 'simplifies' the sampler: on rejection, sample the replacement from p instead of the residual. What happens?
options: Nothing; p and the residual are the same distribution
Outputs become biased toward tokens the draft under-proposes, because their accepted mass is counted twice
Outputs become biased toward tokens the draft over-proposes
Acceptance rate drops but outputs stay exact
explain: Rejection still happens with probability 0.3 in the toy example, but the replacement now follows p, so each token gets min(p, q) + 0.3 p(x): 0.45, 0.26, 0.16, 0.13 instead of 0.5, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1. 'a' and 'dog', which the draft over-proposes, gain mass. The residual sends rejected mass only to under-covered tokens, adding exactly the missing p(x) - q(x).

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: EAGLE drafts and prompt lookup decoding
question: Which drafter fits best for an assistant that rewrites long user-provided code files with small edits, given no budget to train anything?
options: Prompt lookup (n-gram) drafting
A freshly trained EAGLE-3 head
Medusa-2 with a fine-tuned backbone
Typical acceptance with a high threshold
explain: The output copies long spans of the input, which is exactly what n-gram lookup predicts, and it needs no training and costs almost nothing per guess (c near 0). Medusa-2 and typical acceptance also change outputs.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: From 16,000 samples a second to a log-mel spectrogram
question: On the Slaney mel scale, which span covers more mel units: 0 to 1000 Hz or 4000 to 8000 Hz?
options: 0 to 1000 Hz (15 mel versus about 10.1 mel)
4000 to 8000 Hz, because it is four times wider in Hz
They are equal, because the scale is logarithmic everywhere
It depends on the number of mel bands
explain: 0 to 1000 Hz is the linear part: 15 mel. 4000 to 8000 Hz is one doubling in the log region: 27 ln 2 / ln 6.4, about 10.1 mel. So the filterbank spends more bands on the lowest kilohertz, where vowels and pitch live, than on the top four kilohertz. The number of bands only decides how finely the axis is cut.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
question: Window 1 predicts its last complete segment ends at 28.00 s, but the speaker actually finished it at 27.40 s and started a new sentence. What does buffered long-form transcription do next?
options: Starts window 2 at 30.00 s, as always
Starts window 2 at 28.00 s and may skip the words spoken between 27.40 and 28.00 s
Re-runs window 1 with a higher temperature
Averages the two timestamps and starts at 27.70 s
explain: The seek position follows the predicted timestamp, so window 2 starts at 28.00 s and the 600 ms after the true boundary is never transcribed. This is the error propagation between windows that the paper warns about.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns
question: Why is calling munmap on a small buffer often slower in a 64-thread process than in a single-threaded one?
options: The kernel must shoot down stale TLB entries on every CPU running the process, using IPIs and waiting for them
munmap must zero the pages first
Each thread has its own page table that must be edited
munmap takes a global lock across all processes
explain: Threads share one page table, so any CPU running one of them might cache the translation. The initiating CPU interrupts those CPUs and waits for them to flush before the pages can be reused. Threads do not have separate page tables, and freed pages are not zeroed at munmap.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Difference of means: building a vector from contrast pairs
question: You build a CAA vector from 300 pairs where every positive prompt happens to be longer than its negative partner. What is the most likely problem?
options: None: averaging over 300 pairs removes all confounds
The vector partly encodes prompt length, because that difference is consistent across pairs and does not average out
The vector will have length zero
Mean difference only works with exactly one pair
explain: Averaging cancels differences that vary randomly across pairs. A difference that is the same in every pair, such as length, survives averaging and becomes part of the vector. CAA avoids this by making each pair identical except for one answer letter.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Lab: build, sweep and evaluate a steering vector on a small chat model
question: Your hook does `h[:, start:] += vec` where start is the prompt's post-instruction position. Scores look right, but generated text is identical to the unsteered model after the first token. What is wrong?
options: The vector has the wrong sign
Generation recomputes the vector from scratch each step
The model normalizes the vector away at the final layer
With the KV cache each decoding step passes one position, so the slice from start is empty and nothing is added
explain: The first forward pass covers the whole prompt, where the slice works. Later steps see a tensor of length 1, and slicing from a start index of, say, 60 selects nothing. Add to every position when the sequence length is 1, or track absolute positions.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Ingest: MQTT at the edge, a Kafka log in the middle
question: A topic has 4 partitions and a consumer group with 6 consumers. How many consumers receive records?
options: 6: Kafka splits each partition across consumers
1: only the group leader reads
4: each partition goes to exactly one consumer in the group, so 2 sit idle
12: every consumer reads every partition
explain: Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer within a group. With more consumers than partitions, the extras get nothing. Parallelism within a group is capped by the partition count.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
question: Which problem of the basic RNN encoder-decoder did Bahdanau-style attention fix, and which did it leave in place?
options: It fixed sequential computation but kept the fixed-length vector
It removed the fixed-length vector bottleneck but kept the sequential recurrent chain
It fixed both, which is why the Transformer only changed the training recipe
It fixed neither; it only made the model more interpretable
explain: The decoder could now look at every encoder state through a weighted sum, so the single fixed vector stopped being a bottleneck. The encoder and decoder were still RNNs, so computation inside a sequence stayed sequential. The Transformer removed that remaining chain.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Positional encoding and the full encoder-decoder stack
question: You remove the positional encodings from a trained encoder and feed it "dog bites man" and "man bites dog". What happens to the encoder output for the token "man"?
options: It is identical in both sentences
It differs, because attention weights depend on which tokens are nearby
It differs, because the FFN processes positions in order
It becomes all zeros
explain: Without positional information, self-attention and the position-wise FFN are permutation equivariant. Both sentences contain the same three tokens, so "man" gets the same output in each. That is why order must be injected explicitly.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
question: You increase the context length of a model from 4,096 to 16,384 tokens and keep d fixed. Roughly how does the score-matrix work per layer change?
options: It grows about 4 times, like the FFN
It grows about 16 times, while the FFN work grows about 4 times
It stays the same because heads run in parallel
It grows about 2 times
explain: Score work scales with n^2: (16384/4096)^2 = 16. The FFN and projections scale with n, so they grow 4 times. Parallel heads change wall-clock time, not the amount of work.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: BM25 in Lucene and Elasticsearch: fields, tuning, limits
question: An Elasticsearch index has 5 shards and a rare term that happens to be concentrated in one shard. Why might the same document get a slightly different BM25 score than in a single-shard index?
options: IDF and avgdl are computed from per-shard statistics by default
BM25 uses random tie-breaking
k1 is divided by the number of shards
Norms are only stored on the primary shard
explain: Lucene computes N, n_t and avgdl from the index it searches. In Elasticsearch each shard is a separate Lucene index, and the default query_then_fetch search type scores with local, per-shard term and document frequencies. Skewed terms then get different IDFs per shard. The dfs_query_then_fetch search type gathers global frequencies first, at extra cost.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Assemble model.py and check it against GPT-2's real weights
question: After loading GPT-2's weights, your logits differ from Hugging Face's by at most 0.08 and every argmax agrees. Which cause fits best?
options: A missing transpose on attn.c_proj
The MLP uses exact GELU while GPT-2 was trained with the tanh approximation
Weight tying is missing
The causal mask is upper-triangular
explain: The two GELU formulas differ by a few ten-thousandths per activation, which adds up to small logit differences that rarely change the argmax; that is what we measured (0.080). A missing transpose gave a difference of 161.7 and degenerate text, and a flipped mask would leak the future and change the logits wildly.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Making it fast: TF32, bfloat16, torch.compile, fused attention and DDP
question: A run of GPT-2 124M processes 400,000 tokens per second on one GPU with a 989 TFLOP/s bf16 peak. Using 855 million FLOPs per token, what is its MFU?
options: About 86%
About 4%
About 35%
About 12%
explain: 400,000 x 855e6 = 3.42e14 FLOP/s, and 3.42e14 / 9.89e14 = 0.35. MFU compares useful model FLOPs to the hardware peak, the same calculation as for the A100 run.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Many inputs: partial derivatives and the gradient vector
question: A model has 7 billion parameters and a scalar loss. How many numbers are in the gradient of the loss?
options: 1, because the loss is a single number
7 billion, one partial derivative per parameter
About 49 billion billion (7 billion squared), one per pair of parameters
It depends on the batch size
explain: The gradient has one entry per input to the function: here, one partial derivative per parameter. Pairs of parameters appear in the matrix of second derivatives (the Hessian: each entry differentiates one partial derivative again with respect to another parameter; lesson 7), which is far too large to form for such models.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Jacobians: derivatives of vector-valued functions
question: A linear layer maps 512 inputs to 256 outputs, $z = Wx + b$. What are the shapes of the Jacobian $\partial z/\partial x$ and of the gradient $\partial L/\partial W$ for a scalar loss $L$?
options: Both 512 x 256
Jacobian 256 x 512; dL/dW 256 x 512, the shape of W
Jacobian 256 x 512; dL/dW 512 x 1
Jacobian 512 x 512; dL/dW 256 x 256
explain: The Jacobian has one row per output (256) and one column per input (512), and it equals $W$, which is $256 \times 512$. The gradient of a scalar loss with respect to $W$ has one entry per weight, so it matches $W$'s shape; it is the outer product of the 256-entry $\partial L/\partial z$ with the 512-entry $x$.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Expansion and quoting: why rm $f can delete the wrong files
question: In bash, `echo {1,2}-$((3+4))` prints what?
explain: Brace expansion runs first and makes two words, `1-$((3+4))` and `2-$((3+4))`. Arithmetic expansion then evaluates each to 7.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Searching and transforming text: grep, regex, find, sed and awk
question: In a folder containing `a.txt` and `b.txt`, `find . -name *.txt` fails with an error. Why?
options: find does not accept globs after -name
-name needs the full path rather than a pattern
The shell expands `*.txt` to `a.txt b.txt` before find runs, so find gets an extra argument it cannot parse
find refuses to search the current directory
explain: Expansion happens before the command runs (lesson 3). find receives `-name a.txt b.txt`; -name takes exactly one pattern, so `b.txt` is a stray argument. `find . -name '*.txt'` passes the pattern through for find to match against every file name in the tree.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Learning word vectors by predicting their neighbours
question: With window $c = 2$, how many (center, context) pairs does the 6-word sentence *the cat sat on the mat* produce?
explain: Edge words have fewer neighbours: positions 0 and 5 get 2 context words each, positions 1 and 4 get 3, positions 2 and 3 get 4. That is 2 + 3 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 18. The naive 6 x 4 = 24 forgets that the window is cut off at the sentence edges.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
question: A teammate reports that *king - man + woman* returns *king* in your system. What is the best first check?
options: Retrain with a larger dimension
Switch from cosine to Euclidean distance
Whether the nearest-neighbour search excludes the three query words, as the original evaluation did
Increase the number of negative samples
explain: Returning an input word is the expected behaviour when inputs are not excluded: Nissim et al. measured 0.21 accuracy unconstrained vs 0.74 constrained on the same vectors.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Beyond words: autoencoders and the InfoNCE loss
question: A contrastive model is trained with InfoNCE over $N = 256$ candidates per anchor. What is the most mutual information, in nats, that the bound $\log N - L_N$ can certify, however good the encoder?
explain: $L_N \ge 0$, so $\log N - L_N \le \ln 256 = 5.545$ nats (8 bits). 1.386 is $\ln 4$, the limit for 4 candidates; to certify more, use more candidates.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
question: A 13B-parameter FP16 model runs on the same A100 at batch 1. Roughly what is the best-case decode speed?
options: About 78 tokens/s
About 152 tokens/s, the same as 7B
About 24,000 tokens/s
It depends only on the prompt length
explain: Weights are 26 GB; 26 GB / 2.039 TB/s is about 12.8 ms per token, or about 78 tokens/s. Decode time scales with bytes read, so twice the parameters means roughly half the speed.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: When one GPU is not enough: tensor parallelism and the decode floor
question: Which way of using more GPUs lowers the latency of a single decoding request?
options: Tensor parallelism, because each GPU reads only a slice of every layer's weights for the same token
Data parallelism, because there are more copies of the model
Pipeline parallelism, because the layers run on different GPUs
None of them can, since decode is memory-bound
explain: Only tensor parallelism splits the work of one token across GPUs at the same moment, adding their bandwidth together. Data parallelism serves more requests; pipeline parallelism makes one token visit the stages one after another.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The CPU loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat
question: In `addq (%rdi,%rcx,8), %rax`, why is rcx multiplied by 8?
options: Because x86-64 has 8 general-purpose registers
Because the loop is unrolled 8 times
Because memory is read in 8-bit units
Because each long is 8 bytes, so element i starts 8 x i bytes after a
explain: Memory is addressed in bytes, and a long is 8 bytes on x86-64 Linux. a[i] therefore lives at address a + 8 x i. The CPU computes that address as part of the instruction (base rdi plus index rcx times scale 8).

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The OS in charge: system calls and sharing the CPU
question: Why does a system call use a trap instruction instead of letting the program jump directly to the kernel's code for write?
options: Jumps cannot reach addresses that large
Trap instructions are faster than jumps
The trap switches to kernel mode and enters only at handlers the kernel registered, so a program cannot run arbitrary kernel code with full privileges
The C library has no way to call functions
explain: If user code could jump anywhere into the kernel with privileges, it could skip permission checks. The trap table, set up at boot in kernel mode, fixes the only entry points, and the mode switch happens in hardware as part of the trap.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From web crawl to training tokens: the pretraining data pipeline
question: Why did Llama 3 find the document mask mattered more in long-context training than in standard 8K pretraining?
options: A 128K-token sequence packs many unrelated documents, so a plain causal mask lets tokens attend to far more unrelated text
Document masks make attention cost linear in sequence length
Long sequences do not use an end-of-text token
The document mask is needed for the learning rate to anneal
explain: With longer windows a token can see many more tokens from other documents, which can distract or teach false dependencies. The mask keeps each prediction conditioned on its own document only. It changes which keys are visible, not the asymptotic cost.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model
question: During RLHF, the mean reward keeps rising while the KL from the SFT model shoots up and samples start repeating odd phrases. Which change most directly addresses this?
options: Raise beta, or stop at an earlier checkpoint
Lower beta so the policy can explore more
Lower the PPO clip range to 0
Remove the value model
explain: Rising reward with exploding KL is the signature of the policy exploiting the reward model. A larger beta makes drift more expensive, and earlier checkpoints have less drift. Lowering beta makes it worse; a clip range of 0 stops learning entirely.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Building the index: tokens, sorting and postings
question: After indexing, which statistic for a term equals the length of its postings list?
options: Its collection frequency
Its document frequency
Its largest term frequency
The number of positions stored for it
explain: One posting per document that contains the term, so the list length is df. Collection frequency counts every occurrence, which is the sum of the tf values stored in those postings.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Inverted indexes in real engines: compression, updates, Lucene
question: Why does Lucene add documents by writing new segments instead of inserting postings into existing lists?
options: Segments are needed to compute idf
Postings are compressed contiguous runs, so in-place insertion would mean rewriting them; append-only segments plus background merges avoid that
Each segment can only hold one field
Lucene cannot store more than 128 documents per segment
explain: Compressed, gap-encoded postings cannot absorb an insert cheaply. Writing a fresh small segment is fast, and merges later rewrite several segments into one larger, well-compressed segment. This is the same main plus auxiliary idea from the textbook, generalized to many segments. The 128 is the packed block size, not a segment limit.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
question: `int a[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4}; int *p = a + 1;` What is `p[2]`?
options: Undefined, p[2] is past the end
The address of a[3]
explain: p[2] means *(p + 2). p points to a[1], so p + 2 points to a[3], which holds 4. It stays in bounds: the last valid element is a[3].

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Structs and linked data: ->, typedef and a linked list
question: `point a = { .x = 1, .y = 2 }; point b = a; b.x = 9;` What is a.x now?
options: Undefined behavior
It does not compile, because structs cannot be assigned
explain: Struct assignment copies every member, so b is an independent copy. Changing b.x leaves a.x at 1. To share one object, you would use a pointer: `point *p = &a; p->x = 9;` would change a.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Debugging C: gdb and Valgrind on a real crash
question: A crash report shows `#0 nth crash.c:18` and `#1 main crash.c:27`. Which statement is right?
options: main crashed, and nth was the last function it called
The bug must be on line 18, because frame #0 is always the culprit
Line 27 ran after line 18
The crash happened in nth at line 18, called from main at line 27; the cause may be in either
explain: Frame #0 is where execution stopped and #1 is its caller. The faulting line is where the bad pointer was used, not necessarily where the mistake was made: here main passed an index that was out of range.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
question: Which snippet compiles?
options: `let a = &mut s; let b = &mut s; a.push('x'); b.push('y');`
`let a = &s; s.push('x'); println!("{a}");`
`let a = &mut s; a.push('x'); let b = &mut s; b.push('y');`
`let a = &s; let b = &mut s; println!("{a}{b}");`
explain: In option 3, `a` is last used before `b` is created, so the two mutable borrows do not overlap. Option 1 is E0499 (two live `&mut`). Options 2 and 4 are E0502 (a shared borrow is still used after a mutable one starts).

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Structs that borrow: lifetimes in types and what 'static means
question: Does `String` satisfy the bound `T: 'static`?
options: No: only string literals are `'static`
Yes: it owns its data and holds no borrows, even though it is dropped at the end of its scope
Only if it is created at the top of `main`
Only after it is wrapped in a `Box`
explain: A `'static` bound asks that the type contain no short-lived references. Owned data always passes it. Being `'static` as a bound says nothing about how long a particular value lives; the String is still dropped by its owner.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The dot product: one number that measures alignment
question: Two unit vectors have a dot product of 0.5. What is the angle between them?
options: 30 degrees
60 degrees
45 degrees
It depends on their dimension
explain: For unit vectors the dot product equals $\cos\theta$, and the cosine of 60 degrees is 0.5. The formula holds in any dimension, because any two vectors lie in one flat plane (the plane of all their combinations), and the angle is measured inside it.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Determinant and inverse: undoing a map and solving Ax = b
question: For which matrix does $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ have exactly one solution for every $\mathbf{b}$?
explain: The determinants are $4 - 4 = 0$, $10 - 12 = -2$, $6 - 6 = 0$ and $0 - 0 = 0$. Only the second is nonzero, so only it is invertible. A negative determinant is fine: it means the map flips orientation, not that it loses information.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Where it shows up: linear layers, batches and attention scores
question: An `nn.Linear(in_features=768, out_features=3072)` receives a batch of 32 token vectors, shape $32 \times 768$. What are the weight shape and the output shape?
options: Weight 3072 x 768, output 32 x 3072
Weight 768 x 3072, output 32 x 768
Weight 3072 x 768, output 3072 x 32
Weight 32 x 3072, output 32 x 3072
explain: PyTorch stores the weight as (out_features, in_features) = $3072\times768$ and computes $XW^\top$: $(32\times768)(768\times3072) = 32\times3072$. The batch size never appears in the weight.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Mini-batches: noisy gradients and the training loop
question: A training set is stored sorted by label: all cats first, then all dogs. You take minibatches in that order without shuffling. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, since every example is still used once per epoch
The loss becomes non-differentiable
Each minibatch contains a single class, so consecutive gradients pull the model back and forth instead of estimating the full gradient
The learning rate becomes effectively zero
explain: A minibatch gradient is a good estimate only if the batch is a random sample. All-cat batches push toward 'always cat', then all-dog batches push the other way. Shuffling once per epoch fixes it.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Early stopping and why big models still generalize
question: In the degree-9 run, why does held-out error start rising again after about 31,000 steps?
options: The learning rate becomes too large late in training
Gradient descent starts fitting directions that hold mostly noise
The Hessian changes during training
The training loss starts increasing
explain: By then the smooth, signal-carrying directions are fitted. Further progress comes from flatter directions, where the targets' components are mostly noise, so the fit gets better on training points and worse elsewhere. For a linear-in-parameters model the Hessian is fixed, and training loss keeps falling throughout.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Build it: a complete training loop in NumPy
question: A teammate computes mu and sd on all 600 rows instead of the training rows. The test precision barely changes. Why is it still a bug?
options: It is not a bug, since the effect is small
It makes training slower
It changes the decision threshold
Test rows influenced the model, so the test score is no longer a clean estimate; on other data or steps the leak can be large
explain: Preprocessing fit on held-out rows is leakage (lesson 11). For a mean and standard deviation on 600 similar rows the effect happens to be small, but the test score is no longer computed on data the pipeline never saw, and the same habit with feature selection inflated accuracy from 0.48 to 0.87.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backpropagation through a whole network, by hand
question: A hidden unit receives input $x_k = 0$ for this example. What is the gradient of the loss with respect to the weight from $x_k$ into that unit, for this example?
options: Equal to the unit's error delta
0, because BP4 multiplies the error by the input activation
Undefined
The same as the bias gradient
explain: BP4: $\partial L/\partial W_{jk} = a_k \delta_j$. If the input on that edge is 0, the weight had no effect on the output for this example, so its gradient is 0. The bias of the unit still gets $\delta_j$.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Build it: a tiny autograd engine from scratch
question: You add a `relu` method to `Value` with `out = Value(max(0, self.data), (self,))`. Which closure is correct?
options: `self.grad = out.grad`
`self.grad += out.grad`
`self.grad += (self.data > 0) * out.grad`
`self.grad += max(0, out.grad)`
explain: ReLU is the max gate: it passes the upstream gradient when the input was positive and blocks it otherwise, and like every rule it must accumulate with `+=`. micrograd's own relu uses the same test on its output, `(out.data > 0) * out.grad`. Option 4 clips the *gradient*, which is a different (wrong) operation.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: paging, page tables and the TLB
question: Why does a multi-level page table make a TLB miss more expensive than a linear page table?
options: The TLB must be flushed after each lookup
The walk needs a load from the page directory and then from the page of PTEs, instead of one load
Multi-level tables are stored on disk
Each level must be translated by the TLB first
explain: A linear table needs one memory reference to fetch the PTE. A two-level table first reads the page directory entry to find the right page of the page table, then reads the PTE: two loads. It is a time-space trade-off; on a TLB hit the cost is identical.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Waiting for something: condition variables and semaphores
question: Why does `pthread_cond_wait` take the mutex as an argument?
options: So it can release the mutex and put the thread to sleep as one atomic step, then re-acquire it before returning
So the woken thread is guaranteed to run before any other thread
Because condition variables are implemented as mutexes
So it can free the mutex permanently once the condition is true
explain: If the thread released the mutex itself and then slept, a signal could arrive in the gap and be lost. Doing both atomically closes that window. Waking does not guarantee running first: that would be Hoare semantics, and pthreads uses Mesa semantics.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Files and directories: the API and how vsfs finds your data
question: An inode has 12 direct pointers and one indirect pointer; blocks are 4 KB and disk addresses 4 bytes. What is the largest file it can describe?
options: 48 KB
4 MB exactly
4 GB
explain: The indirect block holds 4096 / 4 = 1024 pointers. Together with the 12 direct ones that is 1036 blocks of 4 KB = 4144 KB. 48 KB is only the direct part; 4 GB needs a double indirect pointer.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayes' rule: why a 90 percent accurate test is often wrong
question: Which change most increases P(sick | positive) for a disease with a 1% base rate, starting from sensitivity 0.9 and false positive rate 0.09?
options: Raise sensitivity to 0.99
Lower the false positive rate to 0.01
Both help equally
Neither, the base rate fixes the answer
explain: Raising sensitivity takes the posterior from 9.2% to about 10%. Lowering the false positive rate to 0.01 takes it to about 48%, because false positives come from the 99% healthy group and dominate the positives.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Covariance, correlation and the multivariate Gaussian
question: Two features have variances 9 and 4 and covariance 3. What is their correlation?
options: 3, the covariance itself
About 0.083, which is 3 / (9 x 4)
0.5, which is 3 / (3 x 2)
explain: Divide the covariance by both standard deviations, the square roots of the variances: 3 / (3 x 2) = 0.5. Dividing by the variances themselves is a common slip.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals, p-values and an A/B test
question: An A/B test reports p = 0.03 for a lift in click rate. Which interpretation is correct?
options: There is a 3% chance the new variant is not better
There is a 97% chance the lift is real
If there were no true difference, a gap this large or larger would occur about 3% of the time
The lift is large enough to matter for the business
explain: A p-value is computed assuming the null is true: it is P(data this extreme | H0), not P(H0 | data). Getting the probability that the variant is better needs a prior and Bayes' rule. And p says nothing about whether the effect size matters.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves
question: Under Chinchilla-style scaling (N and D each proportional to about $C^{0.5}$), your compute budget grows 10x. How should the model size change?
options: Grow about 10x, keeping tokens fixed
Grow about 5.4x
Grow about 3.2x, and tokens about 3.2x too
Stay fixed and train 10x longer
explain: $10^{0.5} \approx 3.16$ for both N and D, and $3.16 \times 3.16 = 10$ recovers the 10x compute. 5.4x is the Kaplan prescription ($10^{0.73}$) from lesson 5. Putting all of it into one knob walks up a wall of the IsoFLOP valley.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Batch size, learning rate and data limits as you scale
question: Early in a run the loss is 4.0; later it is 2.5. By Kaplan's fit, how did the critical batch size change, and what does that suggest?
options: It stayed fixed, because it depends only on model size
It fell, because a better model has smaller gradients and needs smaller batches
It doubled once, from 0.27M to 0.54M tokens
It grew about 9x (0.27M to 2.55M tokens), so a batch that suits late training wastes tokens early
explain: $B_{crit} \approx 2\times10^8/L^{1/0.21}$ tokens gives 0.27M at 4.0 and 2.55M at 2.5. It depends on the loss, not directly on size: as the true gradient shrinks relative to its noise, bigger batches stay useful. Hence the batch ramps in GPT-3 and Llama 3.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Average precision, MAP and MRR: one number for a whole ranking
question: You evaluate a search box that jumps the user straight to a product page (each query has exactly one correct product). Which metric best matches the user's experience?
options: MRR
Recall@1000
MAP over all relevant products
11-point interpolated precision
explain: With exactly one right answer, what matters is how high it appears, which is what reciprocal rank measures. Recall@1000 ignores position. With a single relevant document AP equals RR anyway, and the recall-level machinery of 11-point precision adds nothing.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Searching a corpus: indexing, ANN and vector size
question: You will store 10 million passages as 384-dimensional float32 vectors. Roughly how much memory do the raw vectors need?
options: 1.5 GB
3.8 GB
explain: 10,000,000 x 384 x 4 bytes = 15,360,000,000 bytes, about 15.4 GB, before any index overhead such as HNSW graph links. 3.8 GB would be 1 byte per dimension; 30.7 GB would be 768 dimensions.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Encoding new text: replay the merges in rank order
question: Encode newer with the 10 toy merges. What comes out?
options: new e r _
new er_
n e w e r _
ne w e r _
explain: Pairs present at the start: (n,e) rank 6, (e,w) and others unranked. Merge (n,e), then (ne,w) rank 7 gives new. Remaining pairs (new,e), (e,r), (r,_) are not in the list, so the result is new e r _. No er_ token was learned.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Tradeoffs: vocab size, numbers, languages, glitch tokens, alternatives
question: Your model is weak at multi-digit addition, and you are designing the tokenizer for its successor. Which change most directly targets the problem?
options: Double the vocabulary so more numbers become single tokens
Remove the end-of-text token
Make numbers tokenize consistently, for example one token per digit as LLaMA does
Switch from UTF-8 to UTF-16 bytes
explain: The problem is that the same digits land in different token groupings depending on what BPE happened to merge. Splitting digits individually (LLaMA) or into fixed-size groups (cl100k) gives a consistent structure. A bigger vocabulary makes more numbers single opaque tokens, which hides their digits from the model.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Residual connections: why 56 layers trained worse than 20
question: You stack 100 residual blocks with He-initialized branches and see the activation scale grow about 1.4x per block at init. What is the standard fix?
options: Replace every identity shortcut with a learned projection
Lower the learning rate by 100x
Initialize the last layer (or last BatchNorm gamma) of each branch to zero, so every block starts as the identity
Remove the ReLU from each branch
explain: Adding a branch output about as large as the input doubles the variance, so the scale grows by sqrt 2 per block. Zero-initializing the branch's last scale makes F(x) = 0 at the start; Goyal et al. do this with the last BatchNorm gamma. A lower learning rate does not change the forward pass at init.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm and dropout: train vs eval mode
question: You validate a model with BatchNorm but forget `model.eval()`. Validation accuracy changes when you change the validation batch size. Why?
options: Dropout is still active and BatchNorm is unaffected
The running averages are reset at every forward pass
Gradients are being computed during validation
BatchNorm normalizes with each validation batch's own statistics, so each prediction depends on the other examples in its batch
explain: In train mode BatchNorm uses the current batch mean and variance, so changing the batch composition or size changes each example's output. It also keeps updating the running statistics with validation data. In eval mode it uses the fixed running averages.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Instrumenting a run: gradient norms, update ratios, activation stats
question: You resume a crashed AdamW run from a checkpoint that contains only `model.state_dict()`. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: AdamW keeps no state between steps
The weights are reloaded in fp16
Gradients from before the crash are added to the first new step
Adam's m and v, its step count and the schedule all restart, so the first steps behave like the start of a new run
explain: Adam's state lives in the optimizer's state_dict and the schedule's position in the scheduler's. Without them the moment estimates restart at zero and warmup starts over, a different trajectory from the one you interrupted.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Tuning ef and M, and choosing between HNSW, IVF and PQ
question: You must index 1 billion 768-d vectors on machines with limited RAM. Which choice best fits the constraint?
options: HNSW,Flat, because it has the best recall versus speed
Brute force on GPUs, because it is exact
IVF with PQ codes, because each vector shrinks from 3,072 bytes to around 100
HNSW with a larger M, because more links mean less memory
explain: Raw float32 vectors alone would be about 3 TB, and HNSW,Flat needs them in RAM. IVF,PQ stores about m + 8 bytes per vector (about 104 GB with 96 codes), at some accuracy cost. A larger M increases memory, it does not reduce it.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Typosquatting and dependency confusion: winning by name
question: Why does moving internal packages under an npm scope such as @acme defeat dependency confusion?
options: npm refuses to publish scoped packages publicly
A scope maps to exactly one registry, so the resolver never asks the public registry for @acme packages
Scoped names are encrypted
Scoped packages cannot have install scripts
explain: npm's documentation: scopes have a many-to-one relationship with registries; a scope only ever points to one registry. The public registry is simply not consulted for that name. (Also claim the @acme scope publicly so nobody else can.)

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: CI secrets: Codecov and the keys inside every pipeline
question: Codecov's attacker never touched Codecov's git repository. Why didn't that protect anyone?
options: The attacker deleted the repository
Customers downloaded the script from a storage bucket at run time, so the bucket was the real source of truth
GitHub was also compromised
Git repositories cannot store shell scripts
explain: What runs is what is downloaded, not what is in git. The customer who compared the downloaded script with the published hash checked the right thing.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Provenance and SLSA levels: a signed record of how it was built
question: Which attack does SLSA Build L3 provenance NOT protect against?
options: A compromised build step forging the provenance
Modifying an artifact after the build
Uploading a locally built package by hand
A maintainer committing a backdoor to the main branch, which is then built normally
explain: The build was faithful to the source; the source was bad. That needs the Source track (enforced review) and human scrutiny, which is exactly the xz problem.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: xz-utils II: where the payload hid and how it was caught
question: Which distribution practice would have kept the backdoor out of a package even if the 5.6.1 version was adopted?
options: Verifying the maintainer's signature on the tarball
Running the package's test suite
Building the package from the tagged git source instead of the release tarball
Using a newer compiler
explain: The trigger lived only in the tarball. Arch Linux switched xz to build from git when the backdoor was disclosed. The signature was valid (Jia Tan signed it), and the tests passed.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Reproduce collapse yourself: simulate the loops, measure diversity
question: Over five rounds of a synthetic data loop, distinct-2 of the generated set stays near 0.7, but coverage of the rare slice of a held-out real set falls from 0.5 to 0.2. What is the best reading?
options: The generator is fine: distinct-2 is stable, so diversity is preserved
The held-out real set is too small to trust, so ignore it
Diversity is improving, because rare-slice coverage is supposed to fall as quality rises
The phrasing stays varied but rare content is disappearing: the early-collapse signature of losing the tails
explain: distinct-n measures variety inside the generated set, not whether it still covers the real distribution. Falling rare-slice coverage is exactly the tail loss of lessons 1 and 3, which internal metrics can miss.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Synthetic data at scale: rephrasing, textbooks, reward-filtered SFT
question: A synthetic textbook includes a reworded version of a test question from MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding, a 57-subject benchmark). Your decontamination uses 10-gram overlap followed by a SequenceMatcher check. What happens, and what is the sturdier defense?
options: It is caught, because SequenceMatcher compares every sample with every benchmark item
It is caught, because rewording keeps most 10-word runs intact
It does not matter, since contamination only affects pretraining data, not synthetic data
It slips through, since no 10-word run is shared; keep a protected in-house evaluation set the generator never saw
explain: The 10-gram step decides which samples are compared at all, so a paraphrase with no shared 10-gram is never checked. Liu et al. note exactly this gap and recommend safeguarded private benchmarks.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Editing the map: munmap, mprotect, mremap and how exec builds it
question: A program grows a 1 GiB mapping with mremap(p, 1 GiB, 2 GiB, MREMAP_MAYMOVE) and keeps using a pointer it saved earlier, q = p + 4096. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: mremap always grows a mapping in place
If the kernel moved the mapping, q points into the old, now unmapped range, so using it can fault
The first 1 GiB is copied byte by byte, so q sees stale data
mremap fails because MREMAP_MAYMOVE only works on file mappings
explain: With MREMAP_MAYMOVE the kernel may relocate the mapping when there is no room to grow in place, and mremap(2) warns that absolute pointers into the old location become invalid. Use the returned address, or store offsets from the start instead of raw pointers.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When mmap wins, when it hurts, and how to steer it
question: Eight worker processes each need read-only access to the same 2 GiB lookup table on a machine with 64 GiB of RAM. Which approach uses the least memory?
options: Each worker mmaps the file with PROT_READ
Each worker reads the file into its own malloc buffer
Each worker mmaps with MAP_ANONYMOUS and copies the file in
One worker reads it and sends it to the others over a pipe
explain: Read-only file mappings in all eight workers point at the same page cache pages, so the table occupies about 2 GiB once. Reading into private buffers keeps eight copies (16 GiB) plus the page cache copy. Anonymous memory is private per process too. This read-mostly, fits-in-RAM, shared case is where mmap clearly wins.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Taming the tail: hedged requests and honest reporting
question: A colleague says: 'Our load test with wrk2 at 5,000 requests per second shows p99 = 900 ms but production p99 at the same traffic is 20 ms, so wrk2 must be broken.' What is the most likely explanation to check first?
options: HdrHistogram rounds values up by 45x
Production percentiles are always lower than test percentiles
wrk2 sends requests twice
wrk2 measures from intended send times, so if the server cannot sustain 5,000 req/s, queueing builds up and is honestly reported; check that the achieved rate matched the target
explain: If the requested rate exceeds what the system can serve, the backlog grows during the run and every request's latency since its intended time keeps rising. Compare the reported Requests/sec to the -R target and check the test setup (for example, one client machine as bottleneck) before blaming the tool.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Diameter in 4G roaming: the same trust model on IP
question: Your edge sees an Update-Location-Request about IMSI 208010000000042 arriving from a partner realm. Your network is 234-15. What should a category-style rule conclude?
options: Accept: ULRs from partners are always fine
Accept, but only if the subscriber is a VIP
Reject: your HSS is not that subscriber's home, so a ULR for them should not be sent to you
Reject: ULRs are category 1 and never cross networks
explain: A visited MME sends Update-Location to the subscriber's home HSS. IMSI 20801... belongs to network 208-01, not you, so a ULR for it addressed to your HSS has no legitimate purpose. ULRs do cross networks, so they are not category 1.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Inside the 5G core: service APIs, OAuth tokens, SEPP and slices
question: An AMF presents a valid NRF-signed token with scope nudm-sdm, and calls a UDM operation that needs nudm-uecm. What should the UDM return?
options: 403: the token is genuine but does not grant this service
200 OK: any signed token is enough
401: the signature is invalid
It should ask the NRF to widen the scope automatically
explain: Authentication (valid signature) and authorisation (the scope covers this service) are separate checks; TS 33.501 13.4.1 puts the allowed services in the scope claim.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Salt Typhoon: espionage inside carrier networks (2024 to 2025)
question: A router's running config shows the TACACS+ server changed to an address outside your management network. What is the most important concern?
options: The router will boot slower
Administrator logins may now be sent to an attacker, who can capture credentials
SNMP will stop working
The router's clock will drift
explain: AA25-239A reports actors redirecting TACACS+ to their own infrastructure to capture authentication attempts. Treat it as a credential compromise: revert from the golden config, rotate the TACACS+ secret and admin credentials, and hunt for other changes.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Detecting GNSS spoofing, and authenticated navigation signals
question: What does Galileo OSNMA, as operational in 2025, authenticate?
options: The Galileo open-service navigation data (ephemeris and timing parameters), so receivers can verify it came from Galileo unmodified
Every receiver's position
The exact arrival time of every signal at pseudorange level
GPS signals only
explain: OSNMA signs I/NAV navigation data on E1-B. EUSPA says pseudorange-level protection will come from the planned Signal Authentication Service, and GPS L1 C/A data authentication is a future evolution.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Allen relations, current roles and time-scoped queries
question: At month granularity with half-open intervals, role X is Jan 2020 to Jun 2020 and role Y is Jul 2020 to Dec 2020 (both as written, inclusive). Which Allen relation holds for X relative to Y?
options: before, because June is before July
overlaps, because they share the month boundary
during
meets
explain: As half-open intervals X is [2020-01, 2020-07) and Y is [2020-07, 2021-01). X's exclusive end equals Y's start, which is the definition of meets: back-to-back, no gap and no overlap.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Precision: majority vote, best-of-N and when they plateau
question: Your majority-vote accuracy on a math benchmark stops improving between N = 64 and N = 512, but pass@512 (checked against the answer key) keeps rising. What is the most likely reason?
options: Samples become correlated at large N
On the unsolved problems the correct answer is a minority answer, so adding votes reinforces the wrong mode
The model runs out of context window
pass@k is computed incorrectly at large N
explain: Majority vote converges to the mode of the answer distribution. For problems where a wrong answer is the mode, more samples raise coverage but not voting accuracy. That is the plateau Brown et al. report.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
question: DeepSeek-R1-Zero's responses became much longer during RL even though no reward term asked for length. Why is that evidence for test-time scaling?
options: Longer outputs are always rewarded by GRPO
Length was capped at 1,000 tokens
The model copied long human traces
The reward was only for correctness and format, so the model discovered that spending more tokens per problem raised its success rate
explain: R1-Zero's rewards were rule-based accuracy and format rewards. Growth in thinking length alongside accuracy shows the policy learned to buy correctness with test-time tokens.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: A hidden state that is itself a model you train while reading
question: Which of these changes the trained weights of a network itself at inference, instead of a per-sequence state that starts fresh for every input?
options: A TTT-Linear layer reading a 10,000-token prompt
Linear attention accumulating v k-transpose over a document
LaCT updating its SwiGLU fast weights once per 2048-token chunk
Sun et al. (2019): one rotation-prediction gradient step on each test image before classifying it
explain: Sun et al. update the classifier's own shared parameters with a self-supervised loss on the test image. The other three are fast weights: a TTT layer's W, linear attention's state and LaCT's fast weights all start from a learned or zero initial value for each sequence and are thrown away afterwards, while the network's ordinary weights stay frozen.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans' three architectures, worked one segment at a time
question: In MAC, why does segment 3's attention not see the memory update made from segment 3's own tokens?
options: Because the memory is read before the segment is written: h comes from M_2, and the write that adds segment 3 happens after attention
Because MAC never writes segment tokens into the memory
Because persistent tokens block the memory during segment 3
Because the memory is only updated at the end of the sequence
